title: Indian Philosophy: Vedanta and Nyaya Logic
subtitle: You are that, and here is how you know it, and why the materialists said you don't
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the Upanishadic identification of Atman and Brahman, and the meanings of tat tvam asi and neti neti
By the end you will be able to describe Shankara's Advaita Vedanta, including maya, superimposition and levels of reality, and contrast it with Ramanuja
By the end you will be able to lay out the Nyaya theory of pramanas and work through a five-membered inference, identifying vyapti and fallacious reasons
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the Carvaka challenge to inference and compare it with Hume's problem of induction
hook:
A father hands his son a lump of salt and tells him to drop it into a cup of water and come back in the morning. The next day the father asks for the salt. The son looks and cannot find it; it has dissolved. 'Taste the water from this side,' says the father. 'How is it?' Salty. 'From the middle?' Salty. 'From the far side?' Salty. In the same way, the father says, you do not see the subtle essence that pervades everything, yet it is there. That is reality, that is the self. *You are that.*

The scene comes from the *Chandogya Upanishad* (6.13), one of the oldest philosophical texts in the world. It contains the claim that would become the centre of a whole tradition: that the innermost self of each person is identical with the ground of all reality. But Indian philosophy is not one voice. It is a centuries-long argument, conducted in public debates with explicit rules, between mystics and logicians, idealists and realists, believers and materialists. On Day 87 you glimpsed it. In this lesson you will meet three of its participants: Vedanta, which pursues the identity of self and world; Nyaya, which built one of the world's great theories of logic and knowledge; and Carvaka, the materialists who doubted almost everything the others claimed.

sections.heading: From the Vedas to the Upanishads
sections.body:
The oldest Indian texts are the **Vedas**, hymns and ritual manuals composed in Sanskrit from roughly 1500 BCE and transmitted orally with astonishing precision for centuries. The latest layers are the **Upanishads**, a word often explained as 'sitting down near' a teacher. The earliest, including the *Brihadaranyaka* and the *Chandogya*, are usually dated around 800–500 BCE, before or overlapping with the Buddha. They are not systematic treatises but collections of dialogues, debates and teachings, often framed as conversations between teachers and students, kings and sages, husbands and wives.

Their central concern shifts from correct ritual to knowledge. Two terms dominate. **Brahman** is the ultimate reality, the ground from which all things come, in which they live, and into which they return. **Atman** is the self, the innermost subject of experience. The great Upanishadic claim is that these are the same: the deepest self is not a little ego but the very ground of being.

Two famous formulas express this. In the *Chandogya Upanishad* (6.8.7 and refrain), the sage **Uddalaka Aruni** teaches his son Shvetaketu, through the salt and other images, and repeats: **tat tvam asi**, 'you are that'. In the *Brihadaranyaka Upanishad*, the sage **Yajnavalkya** describes the self only negatively, as **neti neti**, 'not this, not this'. The self cannot be grasped as an object, because it is what does the grasping: you cannot see the seer of seeing, he says.

The Upanishads also record women philosophers. In a public debate at the court of King Janaka, **Gargi Vachaknavi** presses Yajnavalkya with question after question about what everything is 'woven upon', until he warns her not to ask too much. Yajnavalkya's wife **Maitreyi** asks whether wealth could make her immortal, prompting his teaching that it is for the sake of the self that all things are dear.

Later Indian thinkers classified schools by their stance toward Vedic authority. The **astika** ('affirming') schools, traditionally six (**darshanas**, 'viewpoints'), include Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta. The **nastika** schools, Buddhism, Jainism and Carvaka, rejected that authority. The classification is a later scheme and hides much cross-fertilisation, but it maps the main lines of debate.

sections.heading: Shankara's Advaita: One Without a Second
sections.body:
**Vedanta**, 'the end of the Vedas', is the family of schools that interpret the Upanishads, the *Brahma Sutras* and the *Bhagavad Gita*. Its most famous exponent is **Shankara** (traditionally dated 788–820 CE, though many scholars place him in the early eighth century). Tradition says he travelled across India debating rival schools and founded monasteries; much of this is hagiography, but his commentaries are among the most studied texts in Indian philosophy.

Shankara's school is **Advaita**, 'non-dualism'. Its thesis is radical: Brahman alone is real, it is pure consciousness without parts or qualities, and the individual self is not a part of Brahman but identical with it. Then why do we experience a world of many separate things and many separate selves? Because of **avidya**, ignorance, which produces **maya**, often translated 'illusion'.

That translation misleads. For Shankara the world is not simply nothing. His central image is the **rope and the snake**. At dusk you see a coiled rope and take it for a snake. Your fear is real, the snake-appearance is real as an appearance, but there is no snake; there is only the rope. When light comes, the snake does not go anywhere; it was never there. Shankara calls this **adhyasa**, superimposition: we project features onto something that does not have them. We superimpose the qualities of body and mind (I am tall, I am sad) onto the pure witnessing consciousness, and then the qualities of pure consciousness (awareness) onto the body and mind.

Advaita therefore distinguishes levels of reality: the **ultimate** (*paramarthika*), Brahman alone; the **empirical** or transactional (*vyavaharika*), the everyday world of tables, people and duties, which is perfectly real for practical purposes; and the **merely apparent** (*pratibhasika*), like dreams and the rope-snake. Compare the Buddhist two truths of the previous lesson, but note the crucial difference: for Nagarjuna nothing has an intrinsic nature, while for Shankara there is one ultimate reality, Brahman, which absolutely does.

Liberation (**moksha**) comes not by ritual or by building merit but by knowledge (*jnana*) that removes ignorance, as light reveals the rope. You do not become Brahman; you discover you always were.

sections.heading: Critics Within Vedanta
sections.body:
Advaita did not go unchallenged, even among those who revered the same scriptures.

**Ramanuja** (traditionally 1017–1137) founded **Vishishtadvaita**, 'qualified non-dualism'. He objected that if ignorance produces the world, whose ignorance is it? It cannot be Brahman's, since Brahman is pure knowledge. It cannot be the individual self's, since on Advaita the individual self is itself a product of ignorance. This dilemma, known as the problem of the **locus of avidya**, has been debated ever since. Ramanuja proposed instead that the world and individual selves are real and are related to Brahman (whom he identified with a personal God, Vishnu) as a body is related to its soul: distinct yet inseparable. Devotion (*bhakti*), not only knowledge, leads to liberation, and liberated souls remain distinct, enjoying God rather than dissolving into identity.

**Madhva** (thirteenth century) went further, founding **Dvaita**, 'dualism', which held that God, souls and matter are eternally distinct.

Notice how these debates parallel Western ones. Shankara's position resembles a strong idealist monism, closer to Plotinus's One (Day 28) or Spinoza's single substance (Day 45) than to Berkeley. Ramanuja's question about the locus of ignorance resembles the problem of evil Augustine faced (Day 30): if all is ultimately good or real, where does the defect come from? But the motivations differ. For all Vedantins, these are not idle puzzles; the right understanding of self and world is the path out of **samsara**, the cycle of rebirth.

sections.heading: Nyaya: The Science of Knowing
sections.body:
Indian debate was a public, rule-governed practice, and **Nyaya** ('rule', 'method') turned it into a systematic theory of knowledge and argument. Its root text, the *Nyaya Sutras* attributed to **Akshapada Gautama**, took shape around the early centuries CE.

Nyaya asks: what are the reliable sources of knowledge? It calls them **pramanas**, 'means of valid cognition', and recognises four:

1. **Pratyaksha**, perception: knowledge produced by contact between sense and object.
2. **Anumana**, inference: knowledge of something not perceived, via something perceived that is invariably connected to it.
3. **Upamana**, comparison or analogy: as when a person told that a wild ox resembles a cow recognises one on first sight.
4. **Shabda**, testimony: the word of a reliable speaker (*apta*), one who knows and has no motive to deceive.

Other schools accepted different lists. Buddhist logicians like Dignaga and Dharmakirti accepted only perception and inference; Mimamsa added more; Carvaka, as we will see, accepted only perception. The question of how many pramanas there are was one of the great organising debates of Indian epistemology.

Nyaya is **realist**: the world exists independently of us and perception, when working properly, puts us in contact with it. It also held that a cognition is shown to be valid **extrinsically** (*paratah*), by checking whether it leads to successful action. If I think there is water ahead and I reach it and drink, my cognition is confirmed. This is strikingly close to modern **reliabilist** and pragmatist theories of knowledge (recall Peirce and James on Day 67).

Indian epistemologists even discussed cases very like Gettier's (Day 74). The Buddhist philosopher **Dharmottara** (c. 8th century) imagined a desert traveller who sees a mirage and judges there is water ahead; when he arrives, there happens by luck to be real water at that very spot. Is his belief knowledge? Many Indian thinkers said no, more than a millennium before Gettier.

sections.heading: Worked Example: The Five-Membered Inference
sections.body:
Nyaya's theory of inference is its masterpiece. The standard illustration is about a hill. Here is the inference stated in the five steps (*avayavas*, 'members') used in public debate:

1. **Thesis** (*pratijna*): The hill has fire.
2. **Reason** (*hetu*): Because it has smoke.
3. **Example** (*udaharana*): Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen.
4. **Application** (*upanaya*): This hill has smoke, which is invariably accompanied by fire.
5. **Conclusion** (*nigamana*): Therefore, the hill has fire.

The technical vocabulary is precise. The hill is the **paksha**, the subject of the inference. Fire is the **sadhya**, the property to be proved. Smoke is the **hetu**, the reason or mark. Everything depends on the relation in step 3, **vyapti**, 'pervasion' or invariable concomitance: smoke is pervaded by fire, meaning there is no case of smoke without fire.

Compare Aristotle's syllogism (Day 17): All smoky things are fiery; the hill is smoky; so the hill is fiery. The logical core is the same. But notice two differences. First, the Nyaya form includes a concrete **example** (the kitchen), anchoring the general rule in experience; inference is treated as a way of extending knowledge from observed cases, not as pure formal deduction. Second, the five steps are designed for persuading an opponent in debate, not just for private reasoning.

Now test your grip on vyapti. Suppose someone argues: the hill has smoke, because it has fire. Is that valid? No. Nyaya logicians answered with a famous counterexample: a **red-hot iron ball** has fire but no smoke. Fire does not pervade smoke; smoke pervades fire only in one direction. A reason that fails like this is a **hetvabhasa**, a 'pseudo-reason'. Nyaya classified these fallacies carefully, for instance a reason that is **inconclusive** (found both where the property is and where it isn't), **contradictory** (it actually proves the opposite), or **unestablished** (it isn't even present in the subject, like inferring fire from 'smoke' that is really mist).

The later school of **Navya-Nyaya** ('new Nyaya'), founded by **Gangesha** (fourteenth century) in his *Tattvachintamani*, developed a highly technical language for stating such relations precisely, which some scholars compare with modern formal logic.

sections.heading: Carvaka: The Materialist Challenge
sections.body:
Not everyone accepted the gods, the self, rebirth or even inference. The **Carvaka**, also called **Lokayata** ('those who follow the world'), were India's materialists. Their own foundational texts are lost, and we know them mostly from hostile summaries by opponents, such as the fourteenth-century compendium *Sarvadarshanasangraha*, so caution is needed: we may be hearing a caricature.

As reported, Carvakas held that only **perception** is a reliable pramana. The world consists of four elements (earth, water, fire, air). Consciousness is not a separate soul but emerges from matter when the elements combine in a body, as the intoxicating power of liquor emerges from fermenting ingredients that individually lack it. When the body dies, consciousness ends. There is no rebirth, no karma carried beyond death, no heaven to purchase with expensive rituals; priests, the Carvakas allegedly said, invented these for their own profit. The sensible goal is a pleasant life, prudently enjoyed.

Their most philosophically powerful argument targets inference. Every inference rests on vyapti: the claim that smoke is *always* accompanied by fire. But how could we know that? Perception tells us only about the cases we have seen, not about all past, future and distant cases. Inference cannot establish vyapti without circularity, since that would use an inference to justify inference. Testimony cannot, since it depends on inference to establish the speaker's reliability. So vyapti, and with it all inference, is never certain.

If this sounds familiar, it should: it is strikingly close to **Hume's problem of induction** (Day 49), stated many centuries earlier. Nyaya replied that we establish vyapti by repeated observation together with the absence of counterexamples, and by a kind of tarka, hypothetical reasoning showing that denying the rule leads to absurdity: if smoke could occur without fire, then smoke would occur without its cause, and we would have no reason to light fires to make smoke. The radical sceptic **Jayarasi Bhatta** (c. 8th century), associated with Carvaka, went further and attacked even perception's credentials, in a work whose title means 'The Lion That Devours All Categories'.

keyQuote.source: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi), Uddalaka Aruni to his son Shvetaketu

modernConnection.title: Is Consciousness Fundamental? Advaita, Cosmopsychism and the Argumentative Indian
modernConnection.body:
Recall the hard problem of consciousness from Day 84: why should physical processes give rise to felt experience at all? A growing minority of philosophers now consider views once dismissed as mystical. **Panpsychists** such as Philip Goff argue that consciousness is a fundamental feature of matter. Some go further to **cosmopsychism**: the cosmos as a whole is the basic conscious subject, and individual minds are aspects of it. The philosopher Miri Albahari and others have explicitly drawn on Advaita Vedanta in developing such views. Erwin Schrödinger, a founder of quantum mechanics, ended his book *What Is Life?* (1944) by endorsing the Upanishadic identity of Atman and Brahman as his own personal view.

The Carvaka, meanwhile, would recognise today's mainstream physicalism, which holds that consciousness emerges from brain activity. Their fermentation analogy is a premodern version of the idea of **emergence**, and it faces the same question the hard problem poses now: is emergence of experience from matter really like the emergence of intoxicating power from grain, or is that analogy hiding the mystery?

The broader lesson concerns stereotypes. The economist and philosopher Amartya Sen, in *The Argumentative Indian* (2005), criticised the Western image of Indian thought as purely spiritual and otherworldly. He pointed to the Carvakas, to formal logic, to public debate traditions, and to the scepticism even in the Rigveda's creation hymn, which ends by wondering whether even the highest overseer knows how the world began, or perhaps does not know. Studying Nyaya alongside Vedanta is a corrective: India produced both the mystic's 'you are that' and the logician's precise rules for when an inference is valid. The comparison with Western panpsychism is illuminating but limited. Advaita's Brahman is not a hypothesis to solve a scientific puzzle; it is realised, the tradition holds, through study, discipline and direct insight.

vocabulary.definition: In the Upanishads and Vedanta, the ultimate reality and ground of all that exists.
vocabulary.example: For Shankara, Brahman is pure consciousness without parts or qualities.

vocabulary.definition: The innermost self or subject of experience, identified in the Upanishads with Brahman.
vocabulary.example: The salt dissolved in water illustrates how atman pervades a person unseen.

vocabulary.definition: In Advaita, the appearance of multiplicity produced by ignorance; neither simply real nor simply nothing.
vocabulary.example: The world as maya is like the snake seen in a rope: experienced, but not ultimately there.

vocabulary.definition: Shankara's term for projecting the features of one thing onto another, as snake-features onto a rope.
vocabulary.example: Saying 'I am tired' superimposes the body's state onto the witnessing self.

vocabulary.definition: A means of valid knowledge, such as perception, inference, comparison or testimony.
vocabulary.example: The Carvakas accepted only one pramana, perception.

vocabulary.definition: Pervasion or invariable concomitance; the universal relation (e.g. wherever smoke, there fire) on which an inference depends.
vocabulary.example: The red-hot iron ball shows that fire does not have vyapti with smoke.

vocabulary.definition: A pseudo-reason or fallacious reason in Nyaya logic.
vocabulary.example: Inferring fire from mist mistaken for smoke commits an unestablished hetvabhasa.

vocabulary.definition: The Indian materialist school, which accepted only perception and denied soul, rebirth and the reliability of inference.
vocabulary.example: The Carvaka argument against vyapti anticipates Hume's problem of induction.

thinkingExercise.title: Hold a Nyaya Debate
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use the Nyaya tools to test an everyday inference, then take the Carvaka's side against it.
steps: Choose an everyday inference you rely on (for example: 'My colleague is upset, because she isn't answering messages'). Write it out in the five members: thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion.
Identify the paksha, sadhya and hetu, and state the vyapti your inference needs. Is it true that wherever the hetu occurs, the sadhya occurs?
Look for a counterexample, your own 'red-hot iron ball'. Which kind of hetvabhasa, if any, does your inference commit?

Finally, argue as a Carvaka: can perception alone ever establish the vyapti? Then argue as Shankara: what in your experience might be superimposed rather than real? Which challenge do you find harder to answer?

summary: The Upanishads (c. 800–500 BCE onward) identify Atman with Brahman, expressed in tat tvam asi ('you are that') and neti neti ('not this, not this').
Shankara's Advaita holds that Brahman alone is ultimately real; the world of many things is maya, produced by superimposition, like a snake seen in a rope.
Ramanuja asked whose ignorance produces maya and defended qualified non-dualism, in which selves and world are real and related to God as body to soul.
Nyaya identified four pramanas and a realist, success-tested theory of knowledge; Indian thinkers discussed Gettier-like cases centuries before Gettier.
The five-membered inference depends on vyapti; fallacious reasons (hetvabhasas) are classified, as in the iron ball that has fire but no smoke.
Carvaka materialists accepted only perception, denied soul and rebirth, and argued that vyapti can never be established, anticipating Hume's problem of induction.

quiz.question: What does Uddalaka's salt-in-water teaching illustrate?
options: That the self is located in the heart
That an unseen essence pervades everything and is identical with one's self
That the world is made of four elements
That knowledge comes only from testimony
quiz.explanation: The dissolved salt, tasted everywhere but not seen, illustrates the subtle essence that is both reality and self: tat tvam asi.

quiz.question: In Shankara's rope-and-snake analogy, what corresponds to the rope?
quiz.explanation: The rope is the one real thing; the snake is the superimposed appearance (the world of multiplicity).

quiz.question: For Shankara, maya means the everyday world is simply non-existent and has no practical reality at all.
quiz.explanation: The everyday world is real at the vyavaharika (transactional) level; it is ultimately non-different from Brahman, like the snake that is really a rope.

quiz.question: Ramanuja's objection about the 'locus of avidya' asks:
options: Where Brahman is located in space
Whose ignorance produces maya, since neither Brahman nor the individual self seems a fitting bearer
quiz.explanation: If Brahman is pure knowledge and the individual self is a product of ignorance, neither can coherently be the bearer of that ignorance.

quiz.question: In the inference 'The hill has fire, because it has smoke', what is the hetu?
quiz.explanation: The hetu is the reason or mark (smoke); the hill is the paksha and fire the sadhya.

quiz.question: Why is 'The hill has smoke, because it has fire' a bad inference in Nyaya terms?
options: Fire does not pervade smoke: a red-hot iron ball has fire without smoke
quiz.explanation: There is no vyapti from fire to smoke; the iron ball is a counterexample, so the reason is inconclusive.

quiz.question: Nyaya held that a cognition's validity is established extrinsically, for example by whether acting on it succeeds.
quiz.explanation: Nyaya's paratah pramanya view checks cognitions by further cognitions and successful action, resembling reliabilist and pragmatist ideas.

quiz.question: A scientist says: 'Every sample we tested reacted, so all samples will react.' Which Carvaka argument most directly challenges this?
options: That vyapti can never be established, since perception only covers observed cases
That testimony is the best pramana
quiz.explanation: The Carvaka argued that universal concomitance cannot be known from finite perceptions, just like Hume's problem of induction.

quiz.question: How does Shankara's view differ from Nagarjuna's, discussed in the previous lesson?
options: Shankara denies any ultimate reality; Nagarjuna affirms one
Both deny that anything has intrinsic nature
Shankara affirms one ultimate reality, Brahman; Nagarjuna denies that anything has intrinsic nature
quiz.explanation: Both distinguish levels of truth, but Advaita affirms Brahman as ultimately real while Madhyamaka holds everything empty of svabhava.

quiz.question: Most of what we know about the Carvaka comes from their own surviving foundational texts.
quiz.explanation: Their foundational texts are lost; we rely largely on summaries by opponents, so we may be reading a caricature.

goDeeper.body:
One of the most exciting areas of contemporary scholarship is the dialogue between classical Indian epistemology and analytic philosophy. Bimal Krishna Matilal (1935–1991), who held the Spalding Chair at Oxford, argued in *Perception* (1986) that Nyaya's debates with Buddhist logicians anticipated many modern disputes about direct realism, sense-data and the role of concepts in perception. Nyaya held that we can perceive universals (like 'cowness') and relations directly; Buddhists such as Dignaga held that pure perception is non-conceptual and that concepts are later constructions. This maps closely onto modern debates about whether perception has conceptual content.

In the theory of knowledge, Stephen Phillips and others have presented Nyaya as an early form of **externalism**: what makes a cognition knowledge is that it was produced by a reliable process, whether or not the knower can prove this. This contrasts with the internalist demand, prominent since Descartes, that one must have access to one's justification.

On the Vedanta side, the debate over the locus of ignorance produced elaborate responses. Later Advaitins split into sub-schools: the Bhamati school located ignorance in the individual soul, the Vivarana school located it in Brahman as its object while denying it touches Brahman's nature. Philosophers today still ask whether non-dual views can explain the appearance of multiplicity without either making it real or making it inexplicable, a problem shared with every monism from Parmenides (Day 5) to modern cosmopsychism, where it is called the **decombination problem**.

questions: Is the Nyaya answer to the Carvaka (repeated observation plus tarka) a better response to the problem of induction than any you have seen from Western philosophy?
If the everyday world is real only at the transactional level, do moral obligations become less binding? How might an Advaitin answer?
Should Western philosophy courses teach Nyaya logic alongside Aristotle? What would be gained?
